claims.text: Integrating metadynamics or umbrella sampling with thermodynamic integration yields accurate melting-temperature predictions for high-entropy alloys.
The integrated method yields accurate predictions of fusion enthalpy and entropy for high-entropy alloys.
The integrated method yields accurate predictions of volume change at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Enhanced sampling combined with thermodynamic integration is computationally efficient across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Atomistic simulations can resolve melting-related structural behavior in a high-entropy alloy.
Metadynamics or umbrella sampling integrated with thermodynamic integration can traverse the free-energy landscape around the melting transition.
Periodic simulations near melting can adequately sample both compositional and thermal fluctuations across diverse high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The resulting atomistic configurations capture free-energy barriers and transition states between solid and liquid phases.
Enhanced sampling overcomes free-energy barriers during melting.
Overcoming the barriers permits accurate integration over the relevant free-energy landscape.
Energetic and volumetric fluctuations during melting govern the targeted thermodynamic properties and can be captured by the proposed method.
The approach will have significantly smaller errors than conventional isolated measurements or simplified models.
Accuracy and efficiency will improve by roughly tens of percent.
The approach applies to near-equiatomic and moderately compositionally varying high-entropy alloys under near-melting conditions.
Extreme compositional ordering or large kinetic barriers may reduce performance by preventing sampling convergence.
Quantitative accuracy and efficiency depend on sampling convergence and the accuracy of the interatomic potentials.
In situ STEM heating can provide validation of melting behavior in a high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle.
Calorimetry, differential scanning calorimetry, high-temperature X-ray diffraction, and viscosity and density measurements can jointly validate all of the specified quantities at high precision.
The approach should be rejected if prediction errors exceed predetermined uncertainty limits or if improvements over conventional methods are not statistically significant.
